opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my main advice is to start by just calling the model API directly. A lot of people reach for a framework on day one, and the trouble is that frameworks add layers of abstraction that hide exactly the things you need to see when you're debugging an agent: what's actually in the prompt, what the tool definitions look like, and what the model got back. When something goes wrong, and it will, you want to be able to look at the raw context and say, "Oh, the model did that because I gave it this confusing instruction," or "this tool description was ambiguous."

The core agent loop is surprisingly simple. You send the model a prompt and a set of tools. It decides to call a tool, you execute that tool, append the result to the conversation, and loop until the model says it's done. That's maybe a few dozen lines of code. Once you've written it yourself, you really understand what's going on, and then if you later adopt a framework, you know what it's doing under the hood and when it's getting in your way.

The other big thing I'd emphasize is to put most of your effort into the tools themselves, what I sometimes think of as the agent-computer interface. People spend a ton of time on the overall prompt and not nearly enough on the tool descriptions, parameter names, and error messages. Treat it like you're writing documentation for a junior engineer on your team. If a smart human would be confused by your tool's docstring, the model will be too. A trick we used a lot was to make tools harder to misuse. For example, we required absolute file paths instead of relative ones, because the model would get lost after changing directories. Small changes like that made a huge difference in reliability.

And finally, start simple and only add complexity when you can measure that it helps. A lot of problems don't need a fully autonomous agent at all. A single well-crafted LLM call, or a simple workflow where you chain a couple of calls together, often gets you most of the way. Reach for the open-ended agent loop when the task really needs that flexibility, and when you have some way to evaluate whether it's actually doing better.

r001.rationale: The response recommends calling the model API directly and implementing the agent loop yourself, but it does not recommend composing utility functions as building blocks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I feel pretty strongly about. When we wrote "Building Effective Agents," the big takeaway was that the most successful teams we saw weren't using the heavy frameworks. They were building with simple, composable patterns directly on top of the model API.

The reason is that frameworks add a layer of abstraction that hides what's actually going into the model. And when you're building an agent, the single most important thing is understanding exactly what the model sees at every step. What's in the context, what tools are available, what the tool descriptions say. If you can't see that because it's buried in six layers of a framework, you're going to spend all your time debugging the framework instead of debugging your prompts.

So my advice would be: start with a direct API call and a loop. Literally, a while loop that calls the model, checks if it wants to use a tool, runs the tool, appends the result, and repeats. That's an agent. That's most of it. You'll be surprised how far that gets you. Then you add things only when you actually hit a problem. If you need to parallelize something, add parallelization. If you need a routing step, add a router. But build it because you have the problem, not because a framework offered it to you.

The other thing I'd say is to spend way more time on your tools than people expect. Treat your tool definitions like you'd treat an API you're handing to a new engineer. Good names, clear descriptions, examples of edge cases. A lot of agent failures that look like "the model is dumb" are actually "the tool description was ambiguous." If you'd be confused reading it, the model will be too.

And honestly, the last point is just to keep it simple for as long as you can. Every piece of complexity you add is something that can go wrong and something that makes the system harder to reason about. The models are getting better fast enough that a lot of the scaffolding people build today will be unnecessary in six months. So the less you've built around the model, the easier it is to swap in a better one and just have everything work.

r001.rationale: The response recommends simple, composable patterns and starting with a direct API call and loop, but it does not clearly recommend composing utility functions as building blocks.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with the simplest thing that could work: call the model directly, give it a few tools, and write the loop yourself. The model asks to use a tool, your code runs it, you pass the result back, and you repeat until it’s done. You don’t need a framework to get that working.

The valuable part is understanding what’s happening at each step. What context does the model see? Are the tool descriptions clear? What happens when a tool fails? When you own that loop, it’s much easier to inspect those decisions and change them.

And I’d be careful about introducing autonomy before you need it. If you already know the steps, just write those steps in code and use the model where you need judgment. Then let the model control more of the workflow as you find tasks where that flexibility actually helps. Start with a concrete task, look at the failures, and add complexity in response to what you learn.

r001.rationale: The response recommends calling the model directly, wiring tools, and writing the loop yourself, but it does not recommend composing utility functions as building blocks.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start with the simplest thing that could work. Call the model directly, give it a few tools, and write a loop: the model asks to use a tool, you execute it, pass the result back, and let it decide what to do next. You don’t need a framework to do that, and having the whole loop in front of you makes it much easier to understand when something goes wrong.

Then add complexity when you have evidence that you need it. Maybe a particular step should be a fixed workflow. Maybe you need better error handling or a way to stop and ask a human. Build those pieces around a concrete task, and look closely at the actual tool calls and results. The goal is to understand what your agent is doing well enough that you can improve it.

r001.rationale: The response recommends a direct model-and-tools loop and adding task-specific pieces, but it does not communicate composing utility functions as building blocks.
